title: Magnetic Particle Testing of Structural Steel and Bridges
description: MT of structural steel and bridge welds to AWS D1.1, AWS D1.5 and FHWA bridge inspection criteria, mobilized across the US. Request a quote with drawings.
h1: Magnetic Particle Testing of Structural Steel and Bridges in the United States
html:
Magnetic particle testing of structural steel and bridges checks fillet and groove welds, connection plates, coped beam ends and crane runway girders for surface cracks, and it is a common tool in bridge magnetic particle inspection of weld details. Atlantis NDT travels to fabrication shops, erection sites, rail and highway bridges and industrial structures across the United States, examines welds to the AWS and owner criteria you specify, and reports each indication. Request a structural steel MT quote with your drawings and specification.

Where MT fits in structural steel work

Structural steel has visual inspection as its foundation, and MT adds a check for cracks that visual examination can miss: fine toe cracks, crater cracks, cracks in heavy-section welds and cracks that start at stress concentrations. Typical uses include:

  • Percent checks of fillet and groove welds on building frames, as a project's quality plan requires.
  • Complete joint penetration welds in moment connections, column splices and heavy plate girders.
  • Repair welds after gouging out an unacceptable condition, to confirm the excavation was clean.
  • Bridge girders, diaphragms, cross frames, gusset plates and bearing details during fabrication and in-service inspection.
  • Crane runway girders and supporting structure, where repeated loading drives fatigue cracking at welds and cope details.
  • Structural details under repair or retrofit, such as welded cover plate ends and web-to-flange junctions.

MT sees surface and shallow subsurface cracks in ferromagnetic steel. It does not size depth, and it cannot see buried flaws well, so projects that need volumetric examination add ultrasonic testing. Our magnetic particle weld inspection page explains the weld technique in more detail.

Codes and standards in structural work

  • AWS D1.1, the structural welding code for steel, governs most building and structure fabrication, including inspection qualification and acceptance criteria. Its criteria differ for statically loaded and cyclically loaded structures.
  • AWS D1.5, the bridge welding code, written with AASHTO, applies to highway bridges and is typically invoked through state transportation department specifications, which can add or change requirements.
  • FHWA National Bridge Inspection Standards, 23 CFR 650 Subpart C, require bridge inspection programs and special attention to fracture-critical members, whose failure could cause collapse.
  • AISC 360 Chapter N sets quality control and quality assurance roles for steel buildings, separating the fabricator's quality control from the owner's quality assurance.
  • ASME Section V Article 7 and ASTM E709 provide MT technique requirements that specifications call out; see the Article 7 explanation.

The project specification, the state DOT or the engineer of record names the governing code and acceptance level. Where the project calls for a particular procedure, we work to it, and where it does not, our Level III prepares one for approval. See technical procedure development.

Who accepts the weld on a structural project

On building work, the engineer of record, the special inspector named in the project documents or the owner's quality assurance agency decides acceptance. The building code's special inspection program may require an approved agency to be responsible for that role. Atlantis does not offer special inspection agency services under the International Building Code, and we do not act as the building official's required inspector. What we do offer is contracted NDT: performing MT to your procedure and reporting indications, so that your fabricator's quality control, the owner's quality assurance team or the engineer of record can use the data in their decision.

On bridge work, the state transportation department or the bridge owner sets inspector qualifications and acceptance, and fracture-critical members often carry stricter rules on welding, inspection and repair. We report to those criteria.

Fracture-critical members and fatigue details

A fracture-critical member is a steel tension member or tension component whose failure would probably cause part or all of a bridge to collapse. These members receive special attention during fabrication, with enhanced welding procedures, inspection and records, and they receive hands-on attention during in-service inspections. Fatigue-prone details, such as cover plate ends, welded attachments to tension flanges and out-of-plane distortion at web gaps, are common locations for cracks that grow under repeated truck loading.

Magnetic particle testing is useful at these locations because it can show a crack tip and length on a clean weld toe. For in-service work, the bridge owner's inspection program sets what is examined and how often, and cleaning, access and traffic control come from the owner. We examine the locations identified, report their position against the bridge's identification system, and supply photographs and sketches. We do not judge remaining life or load rating; that analysis belongs to the owner's engineer.

Technique in the field

Structural MT is nearly always done with an electromagnetic yoke. The technician cleans the weld and adjacent steel to remove slag, spatter and loose coating, magnetizes in two directions, applies particles and examines under adequate light. In shop settings, fluorescent wet particles under ultraviolet light give high sensitivity. On erection sites and bridges, visible dry powder or visible wet particles in daylight are more practical, since darkness and a power source for ultraviolet equipment are often not available. Procedures record lighting levels, yoke lifting-power checks and part temperature, since cold-weather work can slow particle movement and some suspensions have a minimum working temperature.

Bridge steel often carries multiple coats of paint, sometimes lead-containing. Coating removal and containment are the owner's responsibility under environmental and worker-protection rules, and we need to know before we mobilize. Heavy coating reduces MT sensitivity, so the procedure states the allowed coating thickness and the cleaning required.

Shop fabrication versus field erection and repair

Shop and field examinations pose different problems. In a fabrication shop, welds are examined under controlled lighting, often before shipment, and a failed joint is repaired on the floor with the fabricator's own welders. The usual quality plan assigns the fabricator to perform quality control examinations and the owner's agency to perform verification examinations, and Atlantis can fit either role as a contracted examiner under the procedure you name. In the field, erection welds on columns, beams and splices are made with less control over joint fit-up, preheat and weather, and cracking in restrained joints is a recognized risk, so a crack check before bolting up or painting is a reasonable hold point.

Repair and retrofit work on existing steel adds uncertainty. Old structures may contain steel with unknown chemistry or poor weldability, and welded repairs to riveted or early welded connections can start new cracks. When a repair is made, MT of the excavation before welding and of the finished repair afterward confirms that the defect is removed and that no new crack has formed at the repair toes. Where the existing steel is of unknown weldability, the engineer of record decides whether welding is permitted; our role is to report what the examination shows.

Weather limits matter in both settings. Moisture can wash wet particles off a vertical surface and mask indications, and very cold steel may fall below the working range of the suspension. The procedure sets the working temperature range, and we adjust the technique or the schedule when conditions fall outside it.

What the report contains

  • Structure and member identification, joint or weld ID, and location on a drawing, sketch or bridge element reference.
  • Governing code and edition, acceptance criteria, and procedure number and revision.
  • Equipment, particles, lighting, yoke lifting-power check and calibration status.
  • Surface condition and coating, temperature and weather conditions.
  • Technician name and SNT-TC-1A level, with the Level III who approved the procedure.
  • Indications with position, orientation and length, with photographs, and the result against the named criteria.
  • Repair follow-up examinations and final status of each joint.

What to send for a quote

  • Drawings, weld maps or bridge element list, with joint types, quantities and percentages to be examined.
  • Specification, code edition, acceptance level and any state DOT or owner supplement.
  • Material grades and thickness, and any non-magnetic components.
  • Work location: shop, erection site, bridge over water or traffic, with access, lifts, scaffolds or rope access arranged by others.
  • Coating condition, who removes it and containment requirements.
  • Site address, safety orientation, traffic control and badging requirements.

Planning realities

Structural and bridge work depends on access and weather. Weld toes on a girder over a river need lifts, snooper trucks or scaffolds that someone other than the NDT firm usually arranges, and traffic control may limit work to certain windows set by the owner. Cold, wind and rain affect particles and lighting, and fluorescent work needs enclosures. Technicians travel to your site, and Atlantis has no office near it, so plan lodging and site-access paperwork into the schedule early.

Industry pages cover fabrication, steel, rail and wind structures, and the national magnetic particle testing page lists every location.

Training your own technicians

Fabricators and owners with steady structural work may want their own examiners. Atlantis provides MT Level 1 and MT Level 2 training aligned to SNT-TC-1A, and the written practice development service helps a company set the program under which it certifies its own people.

What we do not do here

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, does not act as an IBC special inspection agency, and does not rate bridges or judge remaining fatigue life. Anything outside MT, PT and UT sits beyond this page. We report indications against your criteria, and your engineer or owner decides.

faq.q: Is MT used on bridge welds?
faq.a: Yes. Owners and state DOTs use magnetic particle testing on weld toes, cover plate ends and other fatigue-prone details, and fabrication specifications often call for it under AWS D1.5. The owner's inspection program sets what is examined.

faq.q: What is the difference between AWS D1.1 and D1.5?
faq.a: D1.1 is the structural welding code for steel buildings and structures; D1.5 is the bridge welding code, developed with AASHTO. They have different inspection and acceptance rules, and state DOT specifications can add further requirements.

A steel tension member or component whose failure would probably cause partial or total collapse of a bridge. The National Bridge Inspection Standards in 23 CFR 650 Subpart C require special attention to these members during in-service inspection.

faq.q: Are you a special inspection agency?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not act as an IBC special inspection agency. We perform contracted magnetic particle testing to your procedure and report indications, and the engineer of record, special inspector or owner decides acceptance.

faq.q: Can you test through paint on steel?
faq.a: Only within the coating limits in the procedure. Thin, well-bonded coatings may be allowed, but heavy coatings reduce sensitivity and must be removed. On bridges, the owner arranges removal and any containment required for hazardous coatings.

faq.q: Does MT find buried flaws in structural welds?
faq.a: Poorly. MT shows surface and shallow subsurface flaws. Buried lack of fusion and inclusions in complete joint penetration welds are found by ultrasonic testing, and many structural programs use both.

faq.q: What does AISC 360 Chapter N cover?
faq.a: It sets quality control and quality assurance requirements for structural steel, including inspection tasks and the separate roles of the fabricator's quality control and the owner's quality assurance. Your project documents say which tasks need NDT.

faq.q: Do you inspect crane runway girders?
faq.a: Yes, we examine welds, cope details and attachments on runway girders and supports with MT and report indications. The owner's engineer judges fatigue life and any repair, since we do not perform that analysis.

faq.q: What do you need to quote structural steel MT?
faq.a: Drawings or weld maps, quantity and percentage of joints, code and acceptance criteria, materials and thickness, access and who provides it, coating status, and the site address with safety, traffic control and badging requirements.

faq.q: Can you work on a bridge over water or traffic?
faq.a: We can examine from lifts, snooper trucks or scaffolds provided under the owner's access plan. Traffic control, rigging and access equipment are arranged by the owner or the contractor, and our technicians comply with the site's safety plan.
